Multiple components that support the HTTP/2 protocol are vulnerable to denial-of-service (DoS). An attacker could cause this by flooding the components with pings, causing the components to consume excessive memory or CPU, which could lead to a DoS.

shortDescription.text: Transitive Dependency: netty-transport 4.1.34.Final from gradle 7.0.3 (CVE-2023-44487 BDSA-2023-2732)

fullDescription.text:
The HTTP/2 protocol contains a flaw related to the stream multiplexing feature that can allow for excessive resource consumption on servers operating implementations of the HTTP/2 protocol. 

The HTTP/2 protocol allows clients to signal to a server to cancel a previously opened stream by sending an `RST_STREAM` frame. Attackers can abuse this stream canceling ability by opening a large number of streams at once immediately followed by `RST_STREAM` frames. In most HTTP/2 implementations this bypasses concurrent open stream limits and causes servers to spend processing time first handling request frames and then performing stream tear downs. For the server, these operations can pile up whereas the attacker client paid minuscule bandwidth and processing costs.

[Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2023-011/), [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/technical-breakdown-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack/) and [Google](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/google-cloud-mitigated-largest-ddos-attack-peaking-above-398-million-rps/) have reported that this vulnerability has been exploited in the wild from August to October 2023.

This vulnerability is listed as exploitable by the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency in their [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog).

fullDescription.text:
The HTTP/2 protocol contains a flaw related to the stream multiplexing feature that can allow for excessive resource consumption on servers operating implementations of the HTTP/2 protocol. 

The HTTP/2 protocol allows clients to signal to a server to cancel a previously opened stream by sending an `RST_STREAM` frame. Attackers can abuse this stream canceling ability by opening a large number of streams at once immediately followed by `RST_STREAM` frames. In most HTTP/2 implementations this bypasses concurrent open stream limits and causes servers to spend processing time first handling request frames and then performing stream tear downs. For the server, these operations can pile up whereas the attacker client paid minuscule bandwidth and processing costs.

[Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2023-011/), [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/technical-breakdown-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack/) and [Google](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/google-cloud-mitigated-largest-ddos-attack-peaking-above-398-million-rps/) have reported that this vulnerability has been exploited in the wild from August to October 2023.

This vulnerability is listed as exploitable by the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency in their [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog).

help.text:
The HTTP/2 protocol contains a flaw related to the stream multiplexing feature that can allow for excessive resource consumption on servers operating implementations of the HTTP/2 protocol. 

The HTTP/2 protocol allows clients to signal to a server to cancel a previously opened stream by sending an `RST_STREAM` frame. Attackers can abuse this stream canceling ability by opening a large number of streams at once immediately followed by `RST_STREAM` frames. In most HTTP/2 implementations this bypasses concurrent open stream limits and causes servers to spend processing time first handling request frames and then performing stream tear downs. For the server, these operations can pile up whereas the attacker client paid minuscule bandwidth and processing costs.

[Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2023-011/), [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/technical-breakdown-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack/) and [Google](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/google-cloud-mitigated-largest-ddos-attack-peaking-above-398-million-rps/) have reported that this vulnerability has been exploited in the wild from August to October 2023.

This vulnerability is listed as exploitable by the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency in their [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog).

## Description
Netty is vulnerable to denial-of-service (DoS) due to a lack of limitation of the amount of RST frames that can be sent within a set amount of time. A remote attacker could exploit this by sending crafted HTTP/2 requests in order to cause resource exhaustion. This has been named the "Made you reset" attack.

## Vulnerabilities(BDSA,CVE)
:yellow_circle: [BDSA-2025-8614](https://openhub.net/vulnerabilities/bdsa/BDSA-2025-8614)([CVE-2025-55163](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-55163)) - Netty Vulnerable to Denial-of-Service (DoS) via Lack of Frame Limits in HTTP/2 Implementation


## Solution
Fixed in version [**4.2.4.Final**](https://github.com/netty/netty/releases/tag/netty-4.2.4.Final) by [this](https://github.com/netty/netty/commit/350da8750a44e7d31bc1bb9957dc006055cdfe35) commit and [**4.1.124.Final**](https://github.com/netty/netty/releases/tag/netty-4.1.124.Final) by [this](https://github.com/netty/netty/commit/009bd17b38a39fb1eecf9d22ea8ae8108afaac59) commit

The latest stable releases can be found [here](https://github.com/netty/netty/tags).

## Workaround
As proposed [here](https://github.com/netty/netty/security/advisories/GHSA-prj3-ccx8-p6x4), 
> A quick and easy mitigation will be to limit the number/rate of `RST_STREAM`s sent from the server. It is also possible to limit the number/rate of control frames sent by the client (e.g. WINDOW_UPDATE and PRIORITY), and treat protocol flow errors as a connection error.

fullDescription.text:
Netty when in use in a Windows application is vulnerable to a denial-of-service (DoS) issue due to a lack of sufficient validation of environment files that are read during the Netty startup sequence.

During the startup sequence, Netty has not yet verified what operating system is in use and attempts to access directories that are not normally present on Windows. An attacker with access to the system on which Netty is running could place large crafted files in the directories that Netty attempts to load and trigger a Java out-of-memory error that results in a crash of the Java based application using Netty.

## Description
Bouncy Castle has a flaw in the way the BC/BCFIPS low-level API handles the specifications required to implement RSA key generation. An attacker can exploit this vulnerability to attack the RSA encryption used for key generation to obtain key pair combinations.

## Vulnerabilities(BDSA,CVE)
:orange_circle: [BDSA-2018-1843](https://openhub.net/vulnerabilities/bdsa/BDSA-2018-1843)([CVE-2018-1000180](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2018-1000180)) - Bouncy Castle Vulnerable to Weakened RSA Key Generation via 'RsaKeyPairGenerator::getNumberOfIterations()' Method


## Solution
Fixed in [**1.60**](https://www.bouncycastle.org/latest_releases.html) by [this](https://github.com/bcgit/bc-java/commit/22467b6e8fe19717ecdf201c0cf91bacf04a55ad) commit and [this](https://github.com/bcgit/bc-java/commit/73780ac522b7795fc165630aba8d5f5729acc839) commit.

## Workaround
Only those that use the BC/BCFIPS low-level API to tweak the certainty values and are not aware of the bug will have an issue. 

To get correct 2^-100 for different RSA modulus sizes, you can work around with the following certainty values which guarantee that the full number of M-R tests is satisfied by the Bouncy Castle API : 

 >= 3072: 100 (not affected) 
else >= 2048: 128 
else >= 1536: 134 
else >= 1024: 116 
else >= 512: 186 
else 100 (not affected) 

Additionally, Bouncy Castle uses `BigInteger` to generate the prime candidates (with certainty 1) which does 1 M-R round plus a "Lucas Lehmer" test. 

RSA keys generated under the JCA/JCE use the default values for certainty, which turn out right due to the extra M-R test in BigInteger.

            - org.bouncycastle:bcprov-jdk15on:1.56

## Description
It was discovered that Bouncy Castle for Java was susceptible to excessive allocation issues due to a lack of an established limit on the size of the name constraints object. An attacker could exploit this by supplying crafted content in order to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) condition. 

**Note:** For an attack to take place the `PKIXCertPathReviewer` class must be in use by the application under attack and the class must be consuming certificate paths of unknown origin without any form of other validation.

## Vulnerabilities(BDSA,CVE)
:large_blue_circle: [BDSA-2025-8573](https://openhub.net/vulnerabilities/bdsa/BDSA-2025-8573) - Bouncy Castle for Java Vulnerable to Denial-of-Service (DoS) via Processing of Large Name Constraint Structures in 'PKIXCertPathReveiwer'



## Solution
Fixed in version [**1.79**](https://github.com/bcgit/bc-java/releases/tag/r1rv79) by [this](https://github.com/bcgit/bc-java/commit/310b30a4fbf36d13f6cc201ffa7771715641e67e) commit and [this](https://github.com/bcgit/bc-java/commit/ff444a479942d88de64004dc82c3ee32a9e9075a) commit.

The latest stable releases can be found [here](https://www.bouncycastle.org/download/bouncy-castle-java/).

## Workaround
Per the Vendor,
> Limiting the size of ASN.1 objects that can be loaded from "the wild" will mitigate the risk of an exploit by automatically putting a cap on the maximum size of a Name Constraints structure that the PKIXCertPathReviewer has to consume.

            - org.bouncycastle:bcprov-jdk15on:1.56

## Description
Netty is vulnerable to HTTP request smuggling due to the improper handling of HTTP requests that possess certain properties. An attacker could cause the back-end to misinterpret the contents of HTTP requests made by clients by supplying their own malicious requests in which the HTTP header fields have been maliciously crafted. This could potentially allow the attacker to bypass authentication mechanisms, or to deliver unexpected content to other application users.

fullDescription.text:
The HTTP/2 protocol contains a flaw related to the stream multiplexing feature that can allow for excessive resource consumption on servers operating implementations of the HTTP/2 protocol. 

The HTTP/2 protocol allows clients to signal to a server to cancel a previously opened stream by sending an `RST_STREAM` frame. Attackers can abuse this stream canceling ability by opening a large number of streams at once immediately followed by `RST_STREAM` frames. In most HTTP/2 implementations this bypasses concurrent open stream limits and causes servers to spend processing time first handling request frames and then performing stream tear downs. For the server, these operations can pile up whereas the attacker client paid minuscule bandwidth and processing costs.

[Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2023-011/), [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/technical-breakdown-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack/) and [Google](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/google-cloud-mitigated-largest-ddos-attack-peaking-above-398-million-rps/) have reported that this vulnerability has been exploited in the wild from August to October 2023.

This vulnerability is listed as exploitable by the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency in their [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog).

fullDescription.text:
The HTTP/2 protocol contains a flaw related to the stream multiplexing feature that can allow for excessive resource consumption on servers operating implementations of the HTTP/2 protocol. 

The HTTP/2 protocol allows clients to signal to a server to cancel a previously opened stream by sending an `RST_STREAM` frame. Attackers can abuse this stream canceling ability by opening a large number of streams at once immediately followed by `RST_STREAM` frames. In most HTTP/2 implementations this bypasses concurrent open stream limits and causes servers to spend processing time first handling request frames and then performing stream tear downs. For the server, these operations can pile up whereas the attacker client paid minuscule bandwidth and processing costs.

[Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2023-011/), [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/technical-breakdown-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack/) and [Google](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/google-cloud-mitigated-largest-ddos-attack-peaking-above-398-million-rps/) have reported that this vulnerability has been exploited in the wild from August to October 2023.

This vulnerability is listed as exploitable by the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency in their [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog).

shortDescription.text: Transitive Dependency: netty-codec 4.1.34.Final from gradle 7.0.3 (CVE-2023-44487 BDSA-2023-2732)

fullDescription.text:
The HTTP/2 protocol contains a flaw related to the stream multiplexing feature that can allow for excessive resource consumption on servers operating implementations of the HTTP/2 protocol. 

The HTTP/2 protocol allows clients to signal to a server to cancel a previously opened stream by sending an `RST_STREAM` frame. Attackers can abuse this stream canceling ability by opening a large number of streams at once immediately followed by `RST_STREAM` frames. In most HTTP/2 implementations this bypasses concurrent open stream limits and causes servers to spend processing time first handling request frames and then performing stream tear downs. For the server, these operations can pile up whereas the attacker client paid minuscule bandwidth and processing costs.

[Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2023-011/), [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/technical-breakdown-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack/) and [Google](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/google-cloud-mitigated-largest-ddos-attack-peaking-above-398-million-rps/) have reported that this vulnerability has been exploited in the wild from August to October 2023.

This vulnerability is listed as exploitable by the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency in their [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog).

help.text:
The HTTP/2 protocol contains a flaw related to the stream multiplexing feature that can allow for excessive resource consumption on servers operating implementations of the HTTP/2 protocol. 

The HTTP/2 protocol allows clients to signal to a server to cancel a previously opened stream by sending an `RST_STREAM` frame. Attackers can abuse this stream canceling ability by opening a large number of streams at once immediately followed by `RST_STREAM` frames. In most HTTP/2 implementations this bypasses concurrent open stream limits and causes servers to spend processing time first handling request frames and then performing stream tear downs. For the server, these operations can pile up whereas the attacker client paid minuscule bandwidth and processing costs.

[Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2023-011/), [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/technical-breakdown-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack/) and [Google](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/google-cloud-mitigated-largest-ddos-attack-peaking-above-398-million-rps/) have reported that this vulnerability has been exploited in the wild from August to October 2023.

This vulnerability is listed as exploitable by the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency in their [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog).

shortDescription.text: Transitive Dependency: netty-handler-proxy 4.1.34.Final from gradle 7.0.3 (CVE-2023-44487 BDSA-2023-2732)

fullDescription.text:
The HTTP/2 protocol contains a flaw related to the stream multiplexing feature that can allow for excessive resource consumption on servers operating implementations of the HTTP/2 protocol. 

The HTTP/2 protocol allows clients to signal to a server to cancel a previously opened stream by sending an `RST_STREAM` frame. Attackers can abuse this stream canceling ability by opening a large number of streams at once immediately followed by `RST_STREAM` frames. In most HTTP/2 implementations this bypasses concurrent open stream limits and causes servers to spend processing time first handling request frames and then performing stream tear downs. For the server, these operations can pile up whereas the attacker client paid minuscule bandwidth and processing costs.

[Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2023-011/), [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/technical-breakdown-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack/) and [Google](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/google-cloud-mitigated-largest-ddos-attack-peaking-above-398-million-rps/) have reported that this vulnerability has been exploited in the wild from August to October 2023.

This vulnerability is listed as exploitable by the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency in their [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog).

A remote attacker could take advantage of this vulnerability by repeatedly sending an unlimited number of 1-RTT CRYPTO frames after previously completing the QUIC handshake.
Exploitation was possible for the duration of the connection which could be extended by the attacker. 
quiche 0.19.2 and 0.20.1 are the earliest versions containing the fix for this issue.

shortDescription.text: Direct Dependency: qlog 0.15.2 (CVE-2024-1410)

fullDescription.text: Cloudflare quiche was discovered to be vulnerable to unbounded storage of information related to connection ID retirement, which could lead to excessive resource consumption. Each QUIC connection possesses a set of connection Identifiers (IDs); see  RFC 9000 Section 5.1 https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9000#section-5.1 . Endpoints declare the number of active connection IDs they are willing to support using the active_connection_id_limit transport parameter. The peer can create new IDs using a NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame but must stay within the active ID limit. This is done by retirement of old IDs, the endpoint sends NEW_CONNECTION_ID includes a value in the retire_prior_to field, which elicits a RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frame as confirmation. An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit the vulnerability by sending NEW_CONNECTION_ID frames and manipulating the connection (e.g. by restricting the peer's congestion window size) so that RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames can only be sent at a slower rate than they are received, leading to storage of information related to connection IDs in an unbounded queue. Quiche versions 0.19.2 and 0.20.1 are the earliest to address this problem. There is no workaround for affected versions.

shortDescription.text: Transitive Dependency: netty-resolver 4.1.34.Final from gradle 7.0.3 (CVE-2023-44487 BDSA-2023-2732)

fullDescription.text:
The HTTP/2 protocol contains a flaw related to the stream multiplexing feature that can allow for excessive resource consumption on servers operating implementations of the HTTP/2 protocol. 

The HTTP/2 protocol allows clients to signal to a server to cancel a previously opened stream by sending an `RST_STREAM` frame. Attackers can abuse this stream canceling ability by opening a large number of streams at once immediately followed by `RST_STREAM` frames. In most HTTP/2 implementations this bypasses concurrent open stream limits and causes servers to spend processing time first handling request frames and then performing stream tear downs. For the server, these operations can pile up whereas the attacker client paid minuscule bandwidth and processing costs.

[Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2023-011/), [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/technical-breakdown-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack/) and [Google](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/google-cloud-mitigated-largest-ddos-attack-peaking-above-398-million-rps/) have reported that this vulnerability has been exploited in the wild from August to October 2023.

This vulnerability is listed as exploitable by the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency in their [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog).

In most HTTP/2 implementations this bypasses concurrent open stream limits and causes servers to spend processing time first handling request frames and then performing stream tear downs. For the server, these operations can pile up whereas the attacker client paid minuscule bandwidth and processing costs.

[Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2023-011/), [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/technical-breakdown-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack/) and [Google](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/google-cloud-mitigated-largest-ddos-attack-peaking-above-398-million-rps/) have reported that this vulnerability has been exploited in the wild from August to October 2023.

This vulnerability is listed as exploitable by the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency in their [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog).

message.text: Multiple components that support the HTTP/2 protocol are vulnerable to denial-of-service (DoS). An attacker could cause this by flooding the components with pings, causing the components to consume excessive memory or CPU, which could lead to a DoS.

Netty is vulnerable to HTTP request smuggling due to the improper handling of HTTP requests that possess certain properties. An attacker could cause the back-end to misinterpret the contents of HTTP requests made by clients by supplying their own malicious requests in which the HTTP header fields have been maliciously crafted. This could potentially allow the attacker to bypass authentication mechanisms, or to deliver unexpected content to other application users.

The HTTP/2 protocol contains a flaw related to the stream multiplexing feature that can allow for excessive resource consumption on servers operating implementations of the HTTP/2 protocol. 

The HTTP/2 protocol allows clients to signal to a server to cancel a previously opened stream by sending an `RST_STREAM` frame. Attackers can abuse this stream canceling ability by opening a large number of streams at once immediately followed by `RST_STREAM` frames. In most HTTP/2 implementations this bypasses concurrent open stream limits and causes servers to spend processing time first handling request frames and then performing stream tear downs. For the server, these operations can pile up whereas the attacker client paid minuscule bandwidth and processing costs.

[Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2023-011/), [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/technical-breakdown-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack/) and [Google](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/google-cloud-mitigated-largest-ddos-attack-peaking-above-398-million-rps/) have reported that this vulnerability has been exploited in the wild from August to October 2023.

The HTTP/2 protocol contains a flaw related to the stream multiplexing feature that can allow for excessive resource consumption on servers operating implementations of the HTTP/2 protocol.

For the server, these operations can pile up whereas the attacker client paid minuscule bandwidth and processing costs.

The HTTP/2 protocol contains a flaw related to the stream multiplexing feature that can allow for excessive resource consumption on servers operating implementations of the HTTP/2 protocol. 

The HTTP/2 protocol allows clients to signal to a server to cancel a previously opened stream by sending an `RST_STREAM` frame. Attackers can abuse this stream canceling ability by opening a large number of streams at once immediately followed by `RST_STREAM` frames. In most HTTP/2 implementations this bypasses concurrent open stream limits and causes servers to spend processing time first handling request frames and then performing stream tear downs. For the server, these operations can pile up whereas the attacker client paid minuscule bandwidth and processing costs.

Cloudflare Quiche (through version 0.19.1/0.20.0) was affected by an unlimited resource allocation vulnerability causing rapid increase of memory usage of the system running quiche server or client.
A remote attacker could take advantage of this vulnerability by repeatedly sending an unlimited number of 1-RTT CRYPTO frames after previously completing the QUIC handshake.
Exploitation was possible for the duration of the connection which could be extended by the attacker. 
quiche 0.19.2 and 0.20.1 are the earliest versions containing the fix for this issue.

Cloudflare quiche is vulnerable to a denial-of-service (DoS) due to an infinite loop triggered by improper handling of `RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID` frames. This could allow an attacker to exhaust system resources by sending specially crafted frames that exploit a flaw in connection ID retirement logic.

Cloudflare quiche was discovered to be vulnerable to unbounded storage of information related to connection ID retirement, which could lead to excessive resource consumption. Each QUIC connection possesses a set of connection Identifiers (IDs); see  RFC 9000 Section 5.1 https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9000#section-5.1 . Endpoints declare the number of active connection IDs they are willing to support using the active_connection_id_limit transport parameter. The peer can create new IDs using a NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame but must stay within the active ID limit. This is done by retirement of old IDs, the endpoint sends NEW_CONNECTION_ID includes a value in the retire_prior_to field, which elicits a RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frame as confirmation. An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit the vulnerability by sending NEW_CONNECTION_ID frames and manipulating the connection (e.g. by restricting the peer's congestion window size) so that RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames can only be sent at a slower rate than they are received, leading to storage of information related to connection IDs in an unbounded queue. Quiche versions 0.19.2 and 0.20.1 are the earliest to address this problem. There is no workaround for affected versions.

The node-glob CLI functionality is vulnerable to a command injection issue that affects the `-c/--cmd` option as a result of how matched filenames are passed to a shell with `shell: true`.

To exploit this issue, an attacker could submit files with crafted, malicious names to a system or workflow that uses the vulnerable option in the form `glob -c <command> <patterns>`. Matched filenames could then be passed to a shell where `shell: true` enables shell metacharacters in filenames to trigger command injection. This could be abused to achieve arbitrary code execution.

**Note**: This issue is CLI specific. The core glob library API (core glob functions like `glob()`, `globSync()`, async iterators) is not affected.

Guava creates temporary files and directories with insecure default permissions. A local attacker on the machine could learn the contents of sensitive temporary files.

**Note:** It was determined that the initial patch in version [**30.0**](https://github.com/google/guava/releases/tag/v30.0) by [this](https://github.com/google/guava/commit/fec0dbc4634006a6162cfd4d0d09c962073ddf40) commit was inadequate to fully remove the problem of insecure temporary files from Guava. It only marked a function as deprecated, but the functionality still persisted. A new solution has been released.

Guava is vulnerable to authorization bypass due to the use of an insecure temporary directory for certain file creation operations.
